name: Dale Hoffman
role: Owner, custom harvesting and spraying service

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Dale. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that studies how people see changes at work, and nothing you tell me will be linked to your name.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Go ahead. I've got a sprayer waiting, so let's keep it moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing. A better search engine? I already have one of those. It tells me the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Means nothing. I use it now and then to read a chemical label or check a part number. That's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Run the business. Work out whether that new auto-steer upgrade pays for itself. Argue with the bank, same as every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Business as usual.

S0.say: A better search engine? I already have one. It tells me the weather.
S0.think: It means nothing. I use it to check a part number now and then.
S0.do: Runs the business as usual and works out whether the next auto-steer upgrade pays for itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slow is how farming does everything. I'd tell people not to panic, and to keep the government's nose out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer beginners doesn't bother me. I can't find good young operators now anyway. If the machine does more of the thinking, I need fewer of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Price out the self-driving kits every winter. The day the numbers work, I buy one. Not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. If anything, a bit interested.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 'the numbers work' mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pays back in three seasons or less. I can't wait longer than that. All my money is in iron.

S1.say: Farming does everything slowly. Don't panic, and keep the government's nose out of it.
S1.think: I can't find good young operators now. If the machine does more thinking, I need fewer of them.
S1.do: Prices self-driving kits every winter and buys the day one pays back in three seasons or less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The politicians arguing, that's what I'd complain about. Every time they argue, somebody writes a new rule, and somebody like me has to fill it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI does the paperwork, good. Half my headaches are forms. Spray records, permits, insurance. Let the computer fight the computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get one of those assistants doing my spray logs and the billing. My wife does the books, so she'd have to want it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Annoyed at the politics. The tech I'm fine with.

S2.say: Every time politicians argue, somebody writes a new rule and somebody like me fills it out.
S2.think: If AI does the paperwork, good. Let the computer fight the computer.
S2.do: Tries an AI assistant for spray logs and billing, if his wife, who does the books, agrees.
S2.feel: Annoyed at the politics, fine with the tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody's entitled to anybody else's gains. You want to tax the people who built something to pay people who lost a desk job? Not on my dime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Land going up helps me on paper. But a fight like that only ends one way, with bigger government. That scares me more than any computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get my land and equipment in order. Sit down with the accountant about passing things on before some new tax hits. The succession thing I keep putting off, I'd have to face it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about the work. About the people in charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've put off the succession question for a while. Why would this push you to face it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if the rules on handing down a business change, I want it done before they do. And I'm not getting any younger.

S3.say: Nobody's entitled to somebody else's gains. Not on my dime.
S3.think: Land prices help me on paper, but a fight like that ends in bigger government. That scares me more than any computer.
S3.do: Sits down with his accountant to sort out handing on the business before any new tax arrives.
S3.feel: Uneasy about the people in charge, not the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bring them on. If a robot sprayer works all night and never calls in sick, I want one. And don't let the government slow it down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Here's what I wouldn't say out loud. If a farmer can buy his own robot combine, or rent one from the dealer by the acre, why call me? My whole business is that they don't own the big gear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Talk to the dealer about being their operator, the guy who runs their robot fleet in this county. And pay down debt, because I can't be stuck holding old machines nobody wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I'm racing to buy the thing that might put me out of business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So you'd welcome the robots and fear them at the same time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yep. Doesn't change what I'd do. You buy or you get bought.

S4.say: Bring them on. If a robot sprayer works all night and never calls in sick, I want one.
S4.think: If farmers can rent their own robot combine by the acre, they don't need me.
S4.do: Pitches the dealer on running their robot fleet in the county, and pays down debt so he isn't stuck with old machines.
S4.feel: Racing to buy the thing that might put me out of business.
